# Draft:Killing of Heyward Dyer

Heyward Henry Dyer (December 26, 1946 – October 3, 1969) was an American man who was killed in his Whittier, California, apartment when a stray bullet was fired into the floor above him by Vernon police officer Frank Sweeney during a botched no-knock raid. A search warrant for marijuana had been issued for apartments B and D at 8033 Comstock Avenue. The responding narcotics agents, who were found to be intoxicated while executing the warrant, mistakenly raided 8031 Comstock Avenue, the first floor of the building instead, occupied by 50-year-old Florence Mehan and her 12-year-old daughter Susan. Mehan's mistaken apprehension would lead to Dyer, who had occupied a room on the second floor with his wife Linda and infant son Francis, going downstairs to investigate the noises: eventually, the police officers released Mehan and advanced to the second floor to properly carry out the raid. Linda and Francis would join the others in the downstairs living room, with Linda handing Francis to Dyer at some point before the shooting.
Just as the police officers were preparing to raid a separate apartment, Sweeney, who was carrying an AR-15–style rifle, fired a single .223 caliber bullet into the floor. The bullet pierced Dyer's head, killing him instantly, with Francis nearly being injured in the resulting fall. The use of the rifle was not authorized by the California Bureau of Narcotic Enforcement and Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department. In the aftermath of the incident, Sweeney and other officers that had executed the warrant were suspended without pay; despite a coroner's jury's finding of criminality in the killing, the district attorney's office declined to prosecute Sweeney. A later civil lawsuit led to the Dyer family being awarded US$900,000 in compensation.
Background
Heyward Dyer
Heyward Dyer was born on December 26, 1946, in California. Following his graduation from high school, Dyer studied police law and had intended to become a police officer due to his admiration of a friend that served with the Whittier Police Department. Although Dyer passed the required exams, his wife stated in an interview following his death that he was "too light" for the job and instead pursued work as a draftsman for the Standard Oil Company of California.
Trends in law enforcement
Growing public concerns and fears about drug-related crime had played a part in the passage of the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968, as well as the election of Richard Nixon in the 1968 presidential election. The Omnibus Crime Act had, among other provisions, established the Law Enforcement Assistance Administration, a federal government agency that would provide police forces across the country with equipment and funding. In addition, the attitudes of police in Los Angeles County were substantially impacted by events such as the Watts riots in 1965 and the University of Texas tower shooting in 1966: in particular, then-inspector and future chief of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) Daryl Gates would push for greater influence and inspiration from the military in handling emergencies. As such, the LAPD would establish what would be the first SWAT team in the United States, a trend that was quickly replicated across the country and carrying particular impact in Los Angeles County.
